claims.text: Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella reported that the earthquake death toll reached 111, with 87 injured and 61 buildings collapsed.
The mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, declared a state of public calamity, manifest urgency, and a nighttime curfew in several districts.
In the metropolitan area of Pereira, 40 people were reported dead, 65 buildings collapsed, and people were trapped in 15 of them.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa Azin offered Colombia 47 specialized rescuers, search dogs, and equipment.
The US Geological Survey and Colombia's national authority measured the earthquake at magnitude 7.4.
President Abelardo de la Espriella stated that 1,575 homes were damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 18 health centers damaged, and 52 schools damaged across Colombia.
The epicenter of the quake was located near Tatama National Nature Reserve on the eastern border of Choco province, approximately 30 kilometers from Cartago.
The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude 5.0 aftershock under an hour after the primary earthquake.
Civil aviation authorities suspended flight operations at multiple airports, including Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura, and Cali.
In Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell onto the nave during the earthquake.
In 1999, a 6.2-magnitude earthquake near Armenia, Colombia, killed more than 1,100 people.

Donald Trump proposed a 15-point peace plan for Gaza under which Hamas would surrender its weapons, an international stabilization mechanism would form, and Israeli forces would progressively withdraw.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the US proposal, asserting that no Israeli military withdrawal can occur until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.
Israeli military commanders were blindsided by Prime Minister Netanyahu's public rejection of the peace plan after discussing withdrawal plans in Rafah with him days earlier.
US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper visited Israel to urge Israeli officials to move toward ending military operations in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
Prime Minister Netanyahu scaled back airstrikes in Gaza by requiring targeted killings to be authorized by the IDF chief of staff rather than regional commanders.

A senior US official quoted by journalist Barak Ravid stated the White House understood Netanyahu's political needs ahead of Israel's upcoming election and was unbothered by his rhetoric as long as attacks in Gaza remained restrained.
Construction of the first International Stabilization Force base is scheduled to begin in Rafah at the end of August 2026.
Israeli forces currently control more than 60 percent of the territory in Gaza.
More than 73,300 people have been killed during Israel's military offensive in Gaza since October 2023.
A Ukrainian drone strike on Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan, Russia, located about 750 miles from the border, killed at least 13 people.
The Ukrainian strike targeted the Taneco oil refinery, owned by Tatneft, in Nizhnekamsk.
Tatarstan regional head Rustam Minnikhanov stated that nine people died when a drone struck a hostel building.
The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan confirmed that seven of those killed in the Nizhnekamsk attack were citizens of Uzbekistan.
Swedish security service Säpo shut down a Russian intelligence operation that involved three individuals working under diplomatic cover.
Local officials reported that 75 people were injured and one child was killed in the Ukrainian strike on Nizhnekamsk.
Russia's Defence Ministry claimed air defenses intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territory and Crimea.
The World Health Organization reported that a warehouse in Ukraine's Dnipro region was struck twice in 24 hours, destroying $500,000 worth of medical supplies.
Germany announced it will double personnel in its federal police anti-drone unit to 300 following the discovery of an explosive drone at Leipzig-Halle airport.
Estonia's governing coalition lost its parliamentary majority after two MPs left their parties, leaving the government with 50 of 101 seats.
July was the hottest month ever recorded in the contiguous US in 132 years of record-keeping, with average temperatures 3.3°F above the 20th-century average.
Wyoming recorded its hottest July on record, with average temperatures 5.1°F above normal.
Nearly 70 percent of France, covering 67 of 101 departments, was placed under the highest crisis alert level for water-use restrictions.
Météo-France warned temperatures would reach nearly 40°C in southeastern France, following a national record high of 44.3°C set on June 23.
England and Wales recorded their driest July since 1836, with 19 counties in England receiving no rain for the entire month.
Wildfires in southwestern France in July forced the evacuation of 220,000 people from their homes.
The European climate agency Copernicus reported that global extrapolar sea surface temperatures in July reached a record average of 20.96°C.
Western Europe experienced its hottest June and July on record, with average temperatures reaching 21.62°C, or 2.79°C above normal.
Copernicus reported that July for Europe as a whole was the 11th warmest on record, with an average temperature of 20.49°C.
Russia's Supreme Court ruled to uphold a lawsuit by the Rodina party, barring the liberal Yabloko party from competing in upcoming State Duma elections.
Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov stated outside the courthouse that the party intends to appeal the Supreme Court ruling.
An earlier 2026 poll showed Yabloko with 3 percent public support, below the 5 percent threshold required to gain seats in the State Duma.
The Rodina party's lawsuit accused Yabloko of supporting an extremist organization and committing copyright infringement by quoting a Soviet-era song.
Senior Yabloko member Maxim Kruglov was sentenced in June to seven years in prison for social media posts regarding civilian casualties in Ukrainian cities.
Public support for Russia's ruling United Russia party has fallen to 33 percent.
Kremlin critic and Yabloko politician Lev Shlosberg was charged in 2025 with spreading false information about the Russian military.
WHO Africa director Dr. Mohamed Janabi announced that genetic sequencing showed the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo began in February, three months before its official May 15 declaration.
The DR Congo health ministry reported 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.
Dr. Janabi stated that health workers are reaching only about 30 percent of Ebola cases due to insecurity in eastern DR Congo, with the remaining patients dying at home.
The current Ebola outbreak in DR Congo is the fastest-growing on record, reaching 1,000 deaths faster than the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak.
The WHO recommended initiating full-scale human trials for the Ervebo vaccine to assess whether it provides cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain.
Tropical storm Dolphin caused heavy rainfall and local flooding across eastern China after hitting land as a typhoon on Sunday.
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in Taizhou, Zhejiang province, with maximum sustained winds of 151 kph.
Chinese authorities relocated over 900,000 people in Wenzhou, 150,000 in Fujian, and 200,000 in Shanghai due to the storm.
Shanghai's two main airports cancelled 943 flights on Monday after cancelling over 1,300 flights prior to landfall.
Monsoon rains enhanced by Dolphin caused a landslide in Baguio, Philippines, bringing the total death toll in northern Luzon to 15.
A weather station in central Shanghai recorded 313mm of rainfall in 24 hours, the highest 24-hour total in over 150 years of records.
Typhoon Dolphin drove temperatures in Hong Kong to a record high of 36.9°C on Sunday.
In Okinawa, Japan, the storm injured six people and cut power to more than 50,000 buildings.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing changes to the CDC childhood immunization schedule and calling for the MMR vaccine to be split into three separate shots.
Trump's executive order retains full routine recommendations for only six of 17 childhood vaccines, protecting against 11 diseases.
During the signing, Trump claimed that receiving MMR vaccines together could possibly be lethal and attributed high autism rates to vaccine volume.
Republican Senator Bill Cassidy criticized the executive order on social media, writing that the order is wrong and stating that vaccines do not cause autism.
Trump stated in the Oval Office that children should receive vaccines across a series of doctor visits rather than getting multiple shots in one day.
Separate individual vaccines for measles, mumps, and rubella are not currently licensed or available for children in the US.
Trump previously issued a vaccine directive in December 2025, but subsequent HHS policy changes were blocked by a federal court.
Trump announced that his administration will no longer recommend hepatitis B, Covid-19, or influenza vaccines for children.
BJP leaders Babulal Marandi and Aditya Sahu led a protest outside the Jharkhand chief minister's residence demanding a CBI inquiry into exam leaks and were detained by police.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi condemned police violence against peacefully protesting students during a press conference in Delhi.
Thousands of job aspirants clashed with police in Ranchi during a march to the Jharkhand assembly over alleged recruitment exam irregularities.
Police used water cannons, tear gas, and batons to stop student protesters from storming barricades near the state legislature.
Demonstrators noted that a recent Jharkhand recruitment drive attracted nearly 640,000 applications for 2,025 open posts.
The former chair of the Jharkhand Public Service Commission was arrested over exam irregularities, and three commission members resigned.
Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren published an open letter thanking security agencies for handling student protests with restraint and urging students not to fall into political traps.
Protesting student leaders rejected state claims that 98 percent of demands were met, stating the government only cancelled three of the 13 requested exams.
Union Minister JP Nadda accused Rahul Gandhi of spreading misinformation regarding claims that pellet guns were used against student protesters at Jantar Mantar.
The Lok Sabha passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, by voice vote without debate amid persistent Opposition protests.
The bill creates a New Delhi-based National Tribunals Commission consisting of a chairperson and four members (two judicial and two technical members).
The legislation repeals the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, after the Supreme Court struck down key provisions for violating judicial independence.
The proposed bill places 16 tribunals under commission oversight but excludes the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) while including its appellate forum.
An analysis by think tank DAKSH showed Indian commercial tribunals face a backlog of over 356,000 cases worth ₹24.72 trillion, handled by 350 members.
Under the bill, tribunal chairpersons will serve five-year terms up to age 70, and members will serve five-year terms up to age 67.
Establishing and operating the proposed National Tribunals Commission and its secretariat is estimated to cost ₹27.14 crore.
